bendme.headline: Lower your lid. Watch your desktop fold.
bendme.summary: BendMe turns a small movement of your MacBook lid into a live visual effect. Choose a style, start the effect and watch your screen change perspective.
bendme.audience: For MacBook owners who enjoy a playful desktop.
bendme.experienceTitle: Your lid becomes part of the effect
bendme.experience: You gently lower the lid; the desktop bends with it. Open it again to return to the normal view.
bendme.mechanism: A native Swift and Metal renderer uses screen capture and the lid sensor to draw the effect.
bendme.payoff: The effect is the point. It adds a small moment of delight to a familiar machine.
bendme.evidence: BendMe’s public code, built-in artwork renders and the existing MacBook demo are available to inspect.
bendme.barrier: Requires macOS 14+, Apple silicon and a compatible lid sensor. Screen Recording permission is needed. Pause in Appearance or the menu bar.
bendme.demo: Use the supplied lid demo and the two existing shader renders. The video shows physical lid movement; the artwork switch shows the visual states, not live tracking in the website.
bendme.gap: Screen capture stays on the Mac according to the project source. Compatibility should be checked on each supported model; do not promise the global pause shortcut works.
alternatives: A desktop that follows your MacBook lid.
A little lid movement. A visible bend.

resume-ai.headline: You know the work you’ve done. Let’s put it into words.
resume-ai.summary: Resume AI is for those times when you sit down to write a resume and don’t know where to start.
resume-ai.audience: For job applicants turning work experience into an application.
resume-ai.experienceTitle: Start with the experience you already have
resume-ai.experience: You might have notes from different jobs, a few projects you want to mention, and an old resume that no longer says much about you. The idea behind Resume AI is to bring that experience together and help you turn it into a draft.
resume-ai.mechanism: It uses AI-assisted writing to organize your work and skills. From there, you can read through the draft, change the wording and decide what matters for the role you’re applying for.
resume-ai.payoff: A clearer starting point when your experience is easier to remember than to write about.
resume-ai.evidence: The example below shows the intended writing workflow using the same facts in both views. It is an illustration, not output from a running Resume AI service.
resume-ai.barrier: You still need to check that everything is true and sounds like you. The aim is to give you somewhere to start, without making up experience or promising an interview.
resume-ai.demo: Keep the clearly labeled notes-to-draft illustration. It explains the intended input and output but does not prove the production AI workflow.
resume-ai.gap: User supplied resume-ai.winson.codes in the Vercel screenshot; end-to-end access, export formats, pricing and generation behavior have not been verified. Do not add a live CTA until checked.
alternatives: Your work experience, ready for a first draft.
Start your next application with the work you have done.

yabs.headline: I wanted to compare servers without reading the logs over and over.
yabs.summary: YABS gives you benchmark results. I built this visualizer to make those results easier to read when you’re choosing a VPS.
yabs.audience: For developers comparing VPS benchmark results.
yabs.experienceTitle: Make the measurements easier to inspect
yabs.experience: When you’re comparing servers, the specifications only tell you part of the story. I wanted to look at what the machines had actually measured, without going back and forth through terminal output.
yabs.mechanism: The visualizer takes the results from YABS and presents them visually. You can look through the measurements and consider what they mean for the work you want the server to do.
yabs.payoff: Less back-and-forth through terminal logs when comparing test results.
yabs.evidence: The benchmark website and public source repository are linked here. Test results reflect the conditions under which they were recorded.
yabs.barrier: A benchmark won’t tell you exactly how your own app will run. It gives you something to investigate. You can open the project or look through the source code below.
yabs.demo: Capture real YABS output beside the matching visualization. Highlight the same measurement in both so visitors can trace the source of a displayed value.
yabs.gap: No performance figures, supported import formats or workload wins verified for this rewrite.
alternatives: Compare the measurements behind your VPS choice.
Give YABS output a visual view.

arsenal.headline: I didn’t want useful prompts to get lost in old conversations.
arsenal.summary: Arsenal is a place to keep the instructions you want to come back to when you’re building with AI.
arsenal.audience: For developers who reuse prompts across their work.
arsenal.experience: Sometimes you write a prompt that captures what you need really well. Then the conversation moves on, and the next time you need those instructions, you have to find them again.
arsenal.mechanism: That’s what I’m working on with Arsenal: keeping prompts and project context organized around the work they support. When a similar task comes up, you have a starting point you can return to and adapt.
arsenal.payoff: Continuity between development sessions without treating every prompt as disposable.
arsenal.evidence: Arsenal is linked as a prompt-management project. This page describes the project scope; it does not claim measured improvements in AI results.
arsenal.barrier: You’ll still need to give the AI the right context and check what it produces. Having the instructions in one place just makes them easier to keep working with.
arsenal.demo: Record saving an actual development prompt and finding it for a second task. Confirm the available controls before scripting the recording.
arsenal.gap: Sharing, search controls, integrations, sync, pricing and workflow execution have not been verified.
alternatives: Keep the instructions that worked.
Give recurring development prompts a home.

scatter.headline: You drop a ball and wait to see where it lands.
scatter.summary: That’s the idea behind Scatter. I wanted to see how much fun I could get out of a simple physics game.
scatter.audience: For people who enjoy short, playful browser experiments.
scatter.experienceTitle: The fun is in the fall
scatter.experience: You send a ball into the board and watch it bounce through the obstacles. The interesting part is following its path and wondering where the next bounce will take it.
scatter.mechanism: I built the experiment around that anticipation: the fall, the collisions and the moment the ball lands. Then you can try another drop and watch what happens.
scatter.payoff: Anticipation, movement and the satisfaction of seeing the result.
scatter.evidence: This portfolio records Scatter as a physics-based browser game project. A playable build is not linked here.
scatter.barrier: It’s a browser-game project I’m exploring. There isn’t a playable version linked here yet.
scatter.demo: Record one uninterrupted ball drop in the actual build, from input to landing, with its real feedback. Show the board rather than a fabricated game screenshot.
scatter.gap: Public build URL and supported devices have not been verified for the portfolio.
alternatives: See where the next bounce takes you.
One drop, a board full of possibilities.

laundirii.headline: A laundry order involves more than the person placing it.
laundirii.summary: LaunDiri is a team project about connecting the customer, the courier and the laundry shop.
laundirii.audience: For people exploring coordination in a laundry service.
laundirii.experienceTitle: Make the handoffs part of the order
laundirii.experience: Someone requests a laundry service, but there are other people involved in getting that order through. We wanted to make those handoffs part of the app from the beginning.
laundirii.mechanism: The Android project brings the customer’s request, the courier’s part and the shop’s part into one service workflow. We explored how those roles fit together as an order moves between them.
laundirii.payoff: A clearer view of how a service moves between people.
laundirii.evidence: A collaborative Android application project focused on laundry coordination. This page is a walkthrough, not an offer of an operating laundry service.
laundirii.barrier: This is a project we built together. It isn’t an operating laundry service you can book through this page.
laundirii.demo: Capture the same test order from the customer, courier and shop views. Show only handoffs supported by the actual app.
laundirii.gap: Current availability, exact role permissions, order status updates, team contributions and operational rollout need confirmation.
alternatives: One laundry request, more than one person.
Designing the handoffs behind laundry day.

techno-dynamic.headline: Sometimes a lesson leaves you with another question.
techno-dynamic.summary: Techno Dynamic is a team project exploring how course material and AI-assisted content can work together in a technopreneurship course.
techno-dynamic.audience: For learners exploring technopreneurship course material.
techno-dynamic.experienceTitle: Keep the questions close to the lesson
techno-dynamic.experience: We wanted to bring the material a student is reading closer to the questions they might have about it. That became the starting point for this learning-platform project.
techno-dynamic.mechanism: You can explore course material alongside generated content and suggestions based on frequently asked questions. The idea is to give you another way into the subject when you want to understand more.
techno-dynamic.payoff: A way to explore a topic beyond the first piece of course material.
techno-dynamic.evidence: The documented project scope covers AI-assisted course content and suggestions. No learning-outcome study is supplied.
techno-dynamic.barrier: Generated explanations still need checking. We explored a way to support learning; we haven’t established that it improves grades or replaces a teacher’s guidance.
techno-dynamic.demo: Record a real course section with its associated FAQ suggestion and resulting content. Use a verified lesson and retain any review notices.
techno-dynamic.gap: Live access, sources used for generation, educator review and specific team contributions need confirmation.
alternatives: A course page with somewhere to take your questions.
Bring technopreneurship material and questions together.

rad-ai.headline: I wanted to see what an ultrasound classifier returns.
rad-ai.summary: Rad AI puts an image-classification experiment into an interface where you can inspect the model’s response.
rad-ai.experience: A model is easier to explore when you can give it an input and see what comes back. With Rad AI, that input is a suitable ultrasound research image.
rad-ai.mechanism: The interface connects the image to the classification model and shows its output. The project is about making that experimental process something you can inspect.
rad-ai.payoff: A tangible way to inspect what a classification experiment returns.
rad-ai.evidence: The project is documented as an ultrasound-classification prototype. No clinical validation or accuracy figures are supplied.
rad-ai.barrier: This is a research prototype. It hasn’t been clinically validated and must not be used to diagnose someone or make medical decisions.
rad-ai.demo: Use an authorized non-identifying research image and capture its actual model output. Keep the research-only notice visible. Do not invent confidence values.
rad-ai.gap: Model metrics, datasets, evaluation method, current availability and clinical validity are unverified.
alternatives: From an ultrasound image to an experimental prediction.
Put a classification experiment where it can be inspected.
conversation: A model is easier to explore when you can give it an input and see what comes back. With Rad AI, that input is a suitable ultrasound research image.

jungle-guardians.headline: What does a model see when you show it an animal photo?
jungle-guardians.summary: Jungle Guardians is a learning project where you give a classifier an image and look at the category it predicts.
jungle-guardians.audience: For learners exploring computer vision with animal images.
jungle-guardians.experienceTitle: Make classification something you can try
jungle-guardians.experience: I wanted to make image classification easier to explore. An animal picture gives you a familiar starting point: you can look at the image yourself, then compare it with what the model says.
jungle-guardians.mechanism: You choose an image, run it through the classifier and inspect the predicted category. That gives you a way to think about both the prediction and the mistakes a model can make.
jungle-guardians.payoff: A concrete starting point for understanding predictions and mistakes.
jungle-guardians.evidence: Documented as an interactive animal-image classification project. No accuracy benchmark is supplied.
jungle-guardians.barrier: It’s a learning project, so I wouldn’t treat the output as a reliable identification. I haven’t published an accuracy benchmark here.
jungle-guardians.demo: Record a permitted animal image and the actual returned category. Include a real failure case if available, without inventing predictions.
jungle-guardians.gap: Supported categories, training data, evaluation and public access require verification.
alternatives: See what a model makes of an animal photo.
Explore animal classification one image at a time.

contact-manager.headline: Sometimes you just need to find someone’s details.
contact-manager.summary: Contact Manager is a small project about keeping contact records organized and easy to return to.
contact-manager.audience: For people maintaining a collection of contact records.
contact-manager.experienceTitle: Work with the details you need again
contact-manager.experience: I wanted to focus on the everyday work of looking through contacts and maintaining the information you’ve stored. That’s the scope of this app.
contact-manager.mechanism: I used Angular for the interface and Supabase for the data side. The project centers on browsing and managing those records, so you have a place to come back to when you need the details.
contact-manager.payoff: A dedicated place to work with contact information.
contact-manager.evidence: The project is documented as a contact-management application built with Angular and Supabase. No scale or security audit is claimed.
contact-manager.barrier: I’m sharing it here as an application project. There isn’t a public version linked on this page.
contact-manager.demo: Use fictional contact details in an actual build. Show browsing a record and a supported edit, then confirm the saved value before presenting that capability.
contact-manager.gap: Authentication, data access policies, supported edit operations, import/export and live availability need verification.
alternatives: Return to the contact record you need.
Give contact records a focused workspace.
conversation: I wanted to focus on the everyday work of looking through contacts and maintaining the information you’ve stored. That’s the scope of this app.
